title: TA9-18319
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX Sanchez is a citizen of the Dominican Republic who claims Convention refugee status and refugee protection in Canada based on his allege well-founded fear of persecution in the Dominican Republic for Convention reasons and the alleged risk there to his life, risk of cruel and unusual punishment or treatment, or danger of torture.

The Minister has filed a Notice of Intervention alleging that the claimant should be excluded from refugee protection considering that he has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee.

Based on the evidence and submissions, the claimant is a person referred to in section (f) of Article 1 of the refugee Convention and is thereby not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. The claimant is excluded from the refugee determination process.

In 1998, the claimant was convicted in the United States of America (USA) of assault with a weapon and received three years probation. He pleaded guilty to the charge of assault with intent to cause physical harm. In the year 2004, again in the USA, he was convicted of possession with intent to traffic and served five years probation. He appears to have negotiated the guilty pleas on both of these offences.

The claimant explained, with respect to the first conviction from 1998, that he was followed to his room by a woman who propositioned to have sexual intercourse with him for money. When he said no, she left but then returned, kicked and broke his window and thereby injured herself. He added that he struck her with a plastic tube and threw it at her.

On a careful assessment of the evidence in this area of the claim, I find that the claimant's evidence wavered materially and the story that he put forward was fraught with inconsistencies and discrepancies which remained inadequately resolved. For example, he stated that he threw the tube at the woman when she was leaving; however, he also said that he threw it when he was leaving. At one point in his testimony, he stated that she kicked and broke a window whereas he also testified that she also kicked the door. His explanation for this was that he was not sure why he referred to the door, but he knew that she kicked the window.

I reject this explanation and find that it has not been established on a balance of probabilities that the incident occurred in the way alleged or was precipitated by the conduct of the female victim.
The claimant alleged that he has served his sentence in connection with the 1998 crime.

In 2004, the claimant was convicted of possession with intent to sell. His counsel negotiated a guilty plea in exchange for five years probation. He stated that in the year 2003, he sold, one day apart, six grams of cocaine and made a profit of $120. He claims that he never sold cocaine either before or after this. He alleges that he only sold cocaine because he had been unemployed for a two-week period when he was laid off from full-time employment at an XXXXXXXXX which closed down subsequently. The claimant states that he was re-employed at another XXXXXXXXX right away, but during those two weeks of unemployment, he was arrested. He explained that he had told a friend about his mother's illness whereupon the friend offered that he could sell drugs for money. The claimant went on to allege that his mother had suffered a stroke and was very ill. He stated that she needed medication and that he was sending money to his father. He stated that his mother died and that his father was elderly, had back problems and was not working. He added that his sister suffered from epilepsy and was also not working. By the date of the hearing, there was no independent corroboration regarding either his own employment situation or his family's heath status at material times. His explanation for these critical evidentiary shortcomings was that he did not think it necessary to obtain and supply the information.

I reject this explanation and find it significantly inadequate in the highly important circumstances of a refugee claim, and particularly one that engages the issues that have been set out in his claim.

The claimant said that he could obtain and proffer receipts and other records to corroborate the allegations he has made at his hearing. His counsel applied for leave to obtain, gather and submit corroborating documentation to help support these allegations and explanations, seeking one week to do so and submitting that it would not be necessary to reconvene the hearing.

The Panel ruled that it was not established on balance that the claimant had adequately explained the reasons for his failure to do what was now being requested, in a timely manner and well in advance of his hearing. He had been represented at material times by counsel who is a barrister and solicitor having experience presenting immigration and refugee claims. The claimant's assertion that he did not think it necessary to obtain and submit such corroboration is not satisfactory or credible and was not addressed in any way by his counsel in the course of the application.

Extensive corroboration, including numerous affidavits, was filed in connection with the refugee allegations themselves making it clear that the claimant's mind had specifically been turned to the importance of filing supporting documentation in advance. I therefore reject the late disclosure. Furthermore, there were substantial discrepancies between the oral testimony and work history section of the Personal Information Form (PIF)1 relating to the claimant's place and period of employment with the employer by whom he alleged to have been laid off.

In oral testimony, the claimant stated that he was laid off by the XXXXXXXXX in 2003. In the PIF, on the other hand, it states that he worked at that XXXXXXXXX between XXXXX 2001 and XXXXX 2005. His explanation for this discrepancy in an important area of his claim was that he could not recall the exact times.

Again, I reject this explanation and find that it has not been established on sufficient, reliable evidence that the claimant's allegations in this important area of his claim are reliable. It has not been alleged, much less corroborated and established, that the claimant's ability to recall these or any other timeframes or events either in the PIF or hearing has been impaired or compromised for any reason.

Even though the sentences appear to have been served, based on an exhaustive consideration and analysis of all factors, I find that the claimant is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1(f)(b).

Based on a consideration and analysis of all the factors engaged by the issue of exclusion in this case, I find that it has not been established that there were sufficient mitigating factors on which to determine that the claimant's criminal conduct in the USA had not been tantamount to serious non-political crimes in all the circumstances before the Division.

In coming to this conclusion, I have relied heavily on the submissions and reply of counsel for the Minister. In particular, I have been assisted by and agree with her treatment of what constitutes a serious crime in Canada. I find that the crimes committed by the claimant are serious crimes under Canadian law, and the question of whether or not he served one or more of his sentences does not absolve him from the point of view of assessment of exclusion from the refugee determination process and the state of the current Canadian jurisprudence on Article 1(f)(b).
The Division is not required to proceed onto an examination and analysis of the inclusionary elements of the claimant's refugee claim having found the claimant excluded under Article 1(f)(b).

Accordingly, based on the submissions of both counsels and the evidence properly before me, I conclude that the claimant is excluded under Article 1(f)(b) of the Convention as he has committed serious non-political crimes outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee.
